text: Our Time Is Up: Forced Terminations during Psychotherapy Training JEFF Q. BOSTIC, M.D., Ed.D.* LARRY G. SHADID, M.D.** MARK J. BLOTCKY, M.D.*** Psychiatry residents often must terminate psychotherapy before patients complete their treatment goals, introducing a stressful event into the therapist-patient relationship. Determining what, how, and when to an- nounce the impending termination, anticipating patient responses, managing resident reactions and countertransference, and planning the forced termina- tion to the patient's benefit require careful consideration. The literature on forced terminations is reviewed, two cases illustrate common issues encoun- tered, and nine guidelines are described. As health care limitations on psychotherapy proliferate, psychotherapists are increasingly forced to terminate therapy before patients have achieved their treatment goals. Simultaneously, the future role of psychiatrists as psychotherapists is becoming more uncertain, as reimbursement patterns continue to favor pharmacologic treatments by psychiatrists. These exter- nal factors, as well as limitations imposed by shorter training rotations, relocation after completion of training, and changes in emphasis of psychia- try residency programs, have culminated in psychiatry residents now rarely completing therapy cases with planned terminations.^ Instead, forced termination, that is, therapist-initiated termination of therapy because of extratherapeutic parameters, most frequently now occurs, introducing a potent, often stressful event into the immediate therapist-patient relation- ship.^ While forced termination has become increasingly common, this topic has not been addressed as it pertains to psychiatry residents; rather, issues *Child Psychiatry Fellow, Harvard Medical School, Massachusetts General Hospital. Mailing address: Massachusetts General Hospital, 15 Parkman Street, WAC 725, Boston, MA 02114 3139. **Assistant Clinical Professor, University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, Dallas, TX; Faculty, Dallas Psychoanalytic Institute, now in private practice in Dallas, TX. ***Associate Clinical Professor, University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, Dallas, TX; now in private practice in Dallas, TX. AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol. 50, No. 3, Summer 1996 347 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY in forced terminations have been described as they affect experienced psychotherapists. Unlike psychiatry residents, these psychotherapists have usually treated many cases, providing them with a more stable self-image as therapists and greater confidence and familiarity with options for success- fully navigating their patients through this experience. As a result, psychia- try residents, while at greatest likelihood of completing their psychotherapy cases with forced terminations, have been the least provided with guide- lines for handling this situation. Not surprisingly, only 16% of residents report satisfaction with their therapy terminations, and they report that less than 20% of their patients are ready for termination when it occurs.' Simply, forced termination involves different and significant dynamics, requiring some deviations from traditional termination practices. This discussion reviews reactions of patients and residents to forced termina- tion, addresses the pragmatic issues confronting the resident, provides clinical vignettes illustrating peculiarities of forced terminations, and lists guidelines to assist the departing resident. While forced-termination issues have been described primarily in long-term psychotherapies such as psycho- analysis, the principles derived are applicable to any psychotherapy where intense relationships develop. REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE Patient Reactions To patients, forced termination suggests they will lose their therapists, rekindling the helplessness they experienced from arbitrary, unexpected, and "selfish" behavior of earlier parental figures.'' Patients' affective re- sponses usually resemble earUer reactions to similar experiences; they may feel unworthy, believe the therapist does not really care, feel guilty for transference expressions, or complain "nothing ever works out." They commonly respond to the announcement with denial, displacement, acting out, vengeful self-defeating behavior, searches for substitute transference objects, deprecation of the therapy, increases in symptoms, efforts to immediately terminate without exploring their reactions, attempts to in- duce guilt in the therapist, or urges to "get everything out" to quickly finish treatment or to hold onto the therapist.' Patients may also experience forced termination similar to the "stages" of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance described by Kubler-Ross.^ While not all patients experience each stage in this sequence, this may be useful for understanding patients' reactions, and also for understanding some resistant patients being "stuck" in particular reactions toward therapists.^ Moreover, therapists often focus on patients' anger and 348 Forced Terminations resentment, neglecting feelings of abandonment, anxiety, depression, and pain.'' Resident Reactions and Countertransference Whenever two people are alone in a room together, an emotional relationship develops.^ Residents, though, often underestimate their impor- tance to patients and their own bereavement at termination, as they attempt to insulate themselves from the pain inherent in the loss of a powerful relationship.^ In addition, to avoid angering patients who heretofore have been gratifying, residents may delay telling them about termination, ^^'^^ while attaching excessive personal investment to their patients' progress. ^^ Moreover, as the circumstances causing forced terminations often concomi- tantly change the resident's entire caseload (and human network), residents may further be disappointed with new patients who seem to compare poorly to previous "connected" patients. Countertransference is often most disturbing and dangerous during termination.^^ After encouraging patients' trust, residents may experience considerable guilt betraying this trust. This may impede interpretations, toleration of patients' hostility, or acknowledgment of the importance of this relationship to the patients. Thus, residents may attempt to diminish the patients' grief and sadness over the loss or to alleviate their own guilt by ensuring patients are "taken care of" with rapid transfer to another therapist, although fearing judgment by a new therapist.^ At the same time, departing residents may feel patients' progress is dependent on them, almost expecting deterioration.^ Finally, difficult patients may bring out residents' feelings of relief or even sadistic pleasure after a termination announcement. Accordingly, supervision can be particularly beneficial for departing residents during this time.^"* Patients may detect, prior to the announcement of the departure, the turmoil experienced by the resident and even anticipate the forced termina- tion.^^ If patients discern countertransference, consciously or uncon- sciously, the appropriate therapeutic response is to validate that experi- ence.^^ Such an admission indicates honesty, a vital component of the real relationship." RECOMMENDATIONS When to Announce the Termination The more emotionally attached patients have been to their therapists, the greater the psychic trauma and longer the time necessary to help patients cope with their reactions.^ Historically, therapists have provided 349 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY deeply invested patients with three^'^^ to six months'^ notice of forced termination. What to Say Patients experience most difficulty with forced terminations presented as something imposed on the resident by a higher authority, suggesting the resident, too, is a helpless victim,^^ and perhaps revealing the resident's own unresolved "adolescent" issues with authority. When termination results because of resident relocation, disclosing pertinent facts appears to benefit patients. Indeed, to not provide a baseline of real information to patients but instead "disappear" sends an unhealthy message about relation- ships, therapeutic or otherwise,^^ since avoiding or neglecting the real relationship prompts hostile patient responses not based on transference.^^ Specifically, the more the forced termination resembles patients' past losses, the more patients need to know about the departure in order to gain some control over their intense transference feelings and fantasies.^^ The more reality provided patients, the greater the distinction will occur between the real relationship and the transference relationship, thereby helping them cope with the irretrievable loss of this specific relationship and to differentiate rational reactions to this loss from archaic, irrational, and infantile wishes.^' Finally, the more supportive the therapy, the more patients should be encouraged to express reactions already conscious, rather than to explore unconscious fantasies about the termination.^ In addition, providing patients with the opportunity to make decisions regarding continuation of therapy allows them some mastery over the trauma of rejection.^^ When patients test the investment ofthe therapist by advocating immediate termination, exploration with patients of the advan- tages and disadvantages of various options may be most fruitful. Payments, Gifts, and Subsequent Contact Patients may alter therapy payments once forced terminations are introduced. Meanings associated with such changes warrant timely explora- tion by the therapist. Late payment or nonpayment of fees may reflect anger that patients cannot express verbally to the therapist, but may also reflect a wish to continue the relationship by having "unsettled business" persisting between them, a wish to punish the "authority" perceived responsible for forcing termination, or a desire for special treatment to "prove" the resident sees them as special. Similarly, the patients' "need to be remembered" has been described, perhaps reflecting desire to be forever incorporated into the resident's daily reality.^^ Tangible gifts may be presented to the resident but patients' 350 Forced Terminations statements or acts also may subtly be used to this end; for example, patients may investigate becoming therapists themselves or simply comment how important the resident has been to them. Brief letters responding to patients, which do not address specific therapy issues, may assist patients in the transition. Transfer to Another Therapist Transferring patients might be delayed pending observation of how effectively these patients can work through and master reactions to the forced termination. Historically, therapists have referred approximately 33 % 1^ to 66%5 of their patients. If patients are referred, selecting a therapist who matches the way the particular patient was making use of the departing resident has been recommended.^^ Meeting the new therapist while still seeing the departing resident may allow patients to escape the total abandonment of the transference figure.^^'^^ After consulting a new therapist, though, patients frequently return degrading the new therapist while idealizing the depart- ing resident, similar to the child's handling of the death or loss of a parent. ^^ These complaints often lack depth or emphasize trivial aspects and can easily be interpreted to patients, but may also reveal a "good match" warranting validation by the resident. Finally, facilitating continuity of treatment shows concern for patients, enabling them to separate the departing resident from disappointing past figures.'^ Still, sometimes a few weeks or months between therapists may benefit patients as they consoli- date their work with the departing resident without the anxiety of forming and comparing a new relationship.^'' For chronic patients, it may be possible to foster a transference to the clinic rather than the particular resident, with the departing resident introducing the patients to their new therapists.^ Patients prone to develop institutional transference often see therapists as alike and exhibit ritualistic appointment keeping, dependent relationships with therapists, concern for "sameness," and attachment to the institution.-^^-^^ Once transferred, patients may experience subsequent ambivalence about making progress. If they improve with a new therapist, they may feel disloyal to the departing resident; if they deteriorate, they may feel they are failing the new therapist chosen by the departing therapist.^'' How to Conclude a Forced Termination While it may be difficult for the resident and patients to establish closure simply because they are not through with each other,^^ one sign of emotional maturity is the capacity to recognize that loss is occurring, to 351 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY experience and express appropriate affects, to carry through successfully the work of grief and mourning for the lost object and, eventually, to be available for new, meaningful relationships.' At the level of the real relationship, though, the patient and the resident are "through with" each other, so completing this relationship differently can be maturing for the patient. Essentially, patients must choose between avoiding farewells (with the potential for persisting feelings of loss), and letting go of the resident (with the potential for creative new experiences). From the resident, recapitulation of the patient's progress can be invaluable. Specifically, the following areas of progress can be discussed with the patient:^^ 1. Development of the capacity to love and be loved; 2. Changes in symptoms, problems, and areas of conflict; 3. Extent of resolution of precipitating stresses; 4. Indications of improved coping ability; 5. Degree of increased awareness, appreciation, and acceptance of self and others; 6. Progress in daily functioning; 7. Improvements in quality of life; 8. Capacity to observe oneself and analyze situations. Therapy does not end with the termination, as the same techniques and methods practiced in therapy can be invoked by the patient in the continued quest for self-understanding. Reframing termination as a comple- tion in attainment of a new perspective and new skills may enable the patient to continue practicing beneficial self-analysis. CLINICAL VIGNETTES Case 1 V., a 24-year-old woman, began twice weekly psychodynamic therapy complaining of withdrawal from others and persisting sadness since her mother's death five years earlier. After 18 months of therapy, the resident learned he would be leaving, but feared announcing this departure might prematurely stifle V.'s "other important material." With supervision, he recognized his rationalizations and set a specific date when he informed the patient of the impending termination five months prior to leaving. When told, V. responded, "I'll really miss you," inquired where he was going, whom he would treat, and if he had "pursued this." Before naming the relocation city and his treatment population, the resident explored her questions, as she resented his leaving her to "pursue" something else. Feeling she had been an inadequate, disappointing patient, she requested 352 Forced Terminations he "push me harder," wanting to be "completely honest" so that therapy might be completed before he left. This denial of the real situation, that she would not be "perfect" by the termination date, and her efforts to "speed everything up" were interpreted to her. They also were addressing her needs to be "a better patient by being more honest" and her fantasies of this resulting in his "changing [his] mind and staying." His guilt feelings led him to recommend that V. continue with another therapist, but she retorted, "It wouldn't be right to finish with someone else." The resident explored her "betrayal" feelings and connected them to her fear of "forgetting" her mother if she did not continue mourning her but instead "loved" someone else. V. interviewed with other therapists, but complained of differences in office decor. After he interpreted these superficial differences, she admitted she "couldn't be very fair" because of her liking and identification with him; he acknowledged their "good match," and she decided to see another therapist after taking some time off. When the final therapy sessions were scheduled, V. dropped college courses and argued with her boyfriend, but had difficulty expressing her anger toward him. She felt she was such a "bad girl" that everyone ultimately left her, reaffirming her worthlessness. The resident interpreted this acting out in the transference but also connected it to her efforts to avoid "letting go" of her mother by not finishing college and becoming an adult woman who no longer "needed" her mother. V. reworked her mother's death as they connected her death with losing him, while examin- ing differences between her positions then and now. She wondered what she would be "left with" when sadness no longer permeated her memories of her mother. He, however, focused on her anger until supervision enabled him to recognize his countertransference anger from leaving his colleagues and patients; the patient had "moved on" to feelings of disappointment and sadness regarding the termination. When she observed that the resident seemed "upset," he validated her perceptions, admitting he also would "miss" their sessions. In the final sessions, they reviewed V.'s progress in how she had handled his "death" by doing what she wished she had done with her mother. Unlike avoiding her dying mother, she had stayed in the therapy, had described her positive and negative feelings toward him, and had acknowledged the importance of their relationship as she said good- bye. Presenting him with a brass kaleidoscope, V. explained it was for "nurturing me consistently" He thanked her for it, hoped her life would go well, and shook her hand as she exited. 353 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY Case 2 After a second assault of a policeman, T, a 25-year-old man, entered psychodynamic therapy with a female resident. This therapy was intermit- tently supportive, and over the next 18 months, he examined his fears of homosexuality and his anger at women derived from early, persistent abuse by his mother and neglect by his father. When the termination was announced, T. congratulated the resident and expressed appreciation for the therapy. He then introduced multiple, new problems, but avoided dealing with his feelings by canceling the next two appointments with just a few hours notice. T. verbally assaulted a shoe saleswoman 30 minutes before coming to the third session. He denied any distress resulting from the termination and saw no connection between the cancellations, the "fight," and his feelings toward her leaving. While the resident "looked forward to not seeing [the patient]," and wanted to "just let him go," a supervisor explored her countertransference frustration and disappointment and suggested that the acting out was not an effort at premature termination but instead an indication of her importance to T. She phoned T. to suggest meeting to say goodbye and to review his progress. He attended, reporting he felt he was "losing a friend" as his lonely disconnected feelings returned. He described her importance to him as he reviewed his life successes since therapy and feared "going it alone." Despite her interpretations, T. acted out by making dates with women in cities where he traveled, contending he just wanted to have a choice and not feel he was "stuck with" his girlfriend. He wondered "how well [he] was," attempting comparisons to other patients. He "suddenly" proposed to his girlfriend six weeks before therapy terminated. The therapist reframed his success in establishing a meaningful relationship with her and interpreted the transference by his efforts to replace her. Transfer of this patient was initiated following his recognition that his need for an object replacement was now leading to a hurried marriage. She provided T. with several referral names and identified compatible at- tributes of each one, but left the decision of which one to contact and at what point to him. He ultimately contacted another female resident approximately one month prior to their termination and made plans to continue subsequently with that resident immediately following the forced termination. He chose to see both residents the last two weeks before the forced termination and reported he felt "safer making sure everything works out.' 354 Forced Terminations FORCED TERMINATION GUIDELINES Several general guidelines for managing forced terminations can be derived from this review and these cases. Importantly, though, application to each case requires consideration of specific patient variables such as diagnosis, developmental status, intelligence, ego strength, stage of treat- ment, nature of the therapeutic alliance, type and frequency of therapy, meaning of this loss to the patient, and emotional connection between patient and therapist. Moreover, one also must take into account how close the patient already is to termination, the need for subsequent medication independent of therapy, and benefit of beginning another therapy versus completing this "chapter" of work. 1. When announcing termination, residents should provide notice based on the patients' best interests. Patients longer in therapy with more intense relationships require more time for termination, but this must be tempered with how it will affect current treatment. Impulsive patients, for example, may suddenly stop treatment when termination is announced, preventing several months of productive work if notified too early. Typi- cally, though, for patients in therapy over one year, at least three to six months should be allotted to provide sufficient time for topics independent of the announcement, for issues reawakened by the loss, and for reviewing the patients' progress and saying goodbyes. If patients unconsciously detect impending departures, the resident may need to address termination earlier. 2. Regarding "how much to say," the departing resident might best determine what to reveal prior to the announcement. The resident should not divulge this information too quickly, but rather explore the patient's feelings, fantasies, dreams, and expectations. Relatively, general informa- tion such as the relocation area, the population the therapist will treat, and what the resident will be doing professionally might be described. 3. Subsequent material should continue to be evaluated in light of the patients' narrative themes, core conflicts, defensive patterns, and transfer- ences. It is important to not underestimate the impact of the therapy relationship on patients' subsequent material. Patients' subsequent acting out, efforts to "tell" or "fix everything," or desires for premature closure may all reveal intense, but interpretable, feelings of distress. Kubler-Ross' mourning process may provide a useful framework to categorize patient reactions, as the therapy relationship during a forced termination reactivates prior losses and affords the opportunity for rework- ing them. Leaving is invariably painful, although not necessarily harmful, 355 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY for patients. They can only surmise that the resident is leaving them for something more preferred; patients will, among other responses, feel some degree of rejection. The resulting anxiety, rage, depression, helplessness, and abandonment will activate defenses, often primitive, utilized for previous separations. Therapy affords the opportunity of working through this trauma with maturing of the ego and replacement of more primitive defenses by more adaptive responses. Moreover, the differentiation from past experiences may enhance patients' capacity to integrate good and bad parts of objects (the nurturing, caring "good" therapist with the "abandon- ing" therapist.). This is also a unique opportunity for the resident and patient to discuss their feelings about leaving. For the resident to be genuine is a powerful gift, conveying substantial respect for the patient. Being genuine does not suggest being personal or familiar with patients or that the resident should introduce emotions. In contrast, honest validating of emotions experienced or recognized by patients is appropriate. Additionally, physical contact is not usually helpful to patients, but tearfulness and other emotions may be appropriate. 4. Residents' countertransference may similarly be intense and reveal important unconscious conflicts. Signs of countertransference include residents' attempts to deny their importance to patients, to speed up therapy or to attack previously unaddressed issues, to ensure patients are "taken care of" as soon as possible after the termination announcement, to expect certain feelings from patients, to shift away from painful or distress- ing topics brought up by patients, and to not follow up on missed appointments, nonpayment, or patient tardiness. Moreover, the residents' dreams and fantasy material during this period may reflect subtle but significant countertransference themes. Accordingly, supervision during this phase of therapy can be extremely beneficial. 5. Transfer to another therapist may best be facilitated by framing this as a choice for the patient. Although the departing resident may have strong feelings about continued treatment, subsequent treatment may be doomed if the patient does so only to comply with or to please the resident. Providing names of several therapists perceived compatible with the particular patient may be sufficient, and interviews with other therapists, if initiated by the patient, can be supported prior to the termination. Transi- tion sessions with the patient seeing each therapist (separately) may be beneficial. However, patients may benefit from a consolidation period between therapists so that the patient clarifies issues to be addressed with the new therapist. 356 Forced Terminations 6. Concluding remarks by the resident leave lasting imprints on pa- tients, requiring careful consideration prior to the final sessions. Clarifying progress toward treatment goals, recalling changes from the patient's symptoms and behaviors observed early in the therapy, discussing develop- ment of the relationship "in the room" and what worked for the patient, and identifying different more satisfying schemas now employed by the patient, aU specify the benefits obtained from the therapy. Efforts to promote patients' autonomy by encouraging them to determine dates for final sessions and plans after this therapy further empower patients. While empathizing with patients' concerns about "not finishing together," the resident can reframe the situation to emphasize that patients' goals and efforts toward them remain within their dominion. In addition, shifting emphasis from "being cured" to "completing a piece of work" may help patients view their progress more positively, yet accurately. Final comments encouraging continued growth and happiness may be beneficial to patients. 7. Gifts from patients may represent multiple motives. During forced terminations, the resident's own ambivalence surrounding helping but then deserting the patient before therapy completion may interfere with under- standing the meaning of a patient's gift. A patient may be genuinely thankful for even the limited help provided by the resident, and to acknowledge this appreciation is most beneficial to the patient; refusing such a gift would offend the patient and negate the benefits of the therapy even if the therapist feels the therapy unworthy of reward. Considering other motives such as seeking remembrance, covering underlying hostility, or being the best patient is important, but sufficient evidence should be present to warrant interpreting such a motive. 8. Subsequent contact must be balanced between allowing the patient a "transitional object" as the separation actually occurs and inhibiting the patient from moving on to new relationships with available others. If the patient holds on to the departing resident, investment with a new therapist may be severely impeded. Thus, the resident may provide a professional address for letters if the patient requests this, but indicate that responses may be delayed secondary to new responsibilities (indirectly encouraging the patient to likewise invest energy in more accessible resources) and limited in scope. Initial replies to patient letters may prove this by being brief, noninquisitive, supportive of other developing relationships, and kind rather than analytic. It is important to realize that subsequent contact may become more beneficial to departed residents than to patients as subsequent contact primarily provides the residents' periodic recognition of their past significance to patients. Accordingly, as the relationship 357 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY provides less benefit to patients, decreased resident involvement, evi- denced by briefer, less frequent responses to patient letters, may be more appropriate. 9. The last session, unlike that in a regular termination where the therapist remains available for the patient subsequently, may result in the resident feeling a need to find something particularly important to say as this therapy is concluded. Typically, however, the patient has not completed the therapy work, and to attempt perhaps significant but ultimately premature interpretations even at this point provides little, if any, benefit to the patient. It may be beneficial to reframe that "therapy" will continue after this session through the patient's reflecting on work done, recognizing persisting relationship patterns previously identified, and invoking memo- ries of the resident to predict what the resident might say as additional conflicts arise. SUMMARY Forced terminations are a powerful experience for both patients and for residents. Such terminations often resemble earlier losses to patients, who may react with particular defense constellations, changes in symptoms, and profound reactions to the therapist. Similarly, prominent countertransfer- ence may manifest in attempts by residents to deny their importance to patients, to project reactions onto their patients, and to alter the therapy relationship. More intense therapy relationships usually require termina- tion announcements months in advance. How much wiU be revealed to patients may best be determined prior to the announcement. Payments, gifts, subsequent contact, transfer to another therapist, and concluding therapy comments need evaluation of what is in the patient's best interest and may require creative approaches deviating from traditional therapy practices. This discussion reviewed reactions of patients and residents to forced termination, addressed the pragmatic issues confronting the resident, provided clinical vignettes illustrating peculiarities of forced terminations, and listed recommendations to assist the departing resident. Forced termi- nations afford powerful opportunities for contending with abandonment, disappointment, and loss directly in the therapy. While these experiences are certainly not comfortable, they can be used constructively to benefit patients if the issues surrounding the forced termination are carefully considered and addressed within the therapy. 358 Forced Terminations Acknowledgments: The authors thank Drs.
